questions.question: You flip two fair, independent coins. Let S = 'the coins match' and A = 'coin 1 is heads'. Are S and A independent?
options: Yes: Pr[S | A] = Pr[coin 2 is heads] = 1/2 = Pr[S]
No, because S depends on coin 1
No, because S and A overlap
Only if the coins are biased
questions.explanation: An event can involve coin 1 and still be independent of it. Knowing coin 1 is heads leaves the chance of a match at exactly 1/2. With biased coins this usually breaks.

questions.question: Which statement is equivalent to 'A is independent of B' for every pair of events, including when Pr[B] = 0?
questions.explanation: The product rule is equivalent by a proof by cases on whether Pr[B] = 0. Disjointness (with positive probabilities) actually forces dependence.

questions.question: A suspect matches 9 DNA markers, each shared by 10% of people. When is the claim 'one in a billion' justified?
options: Always, because 0.1 to the 9th power is 10⁻⁹
When each pair of markers is independent
When the nine marker events are mutually independent
Never, because probabilities do not apply to individuals
questions.explanation: Multiplying all nine probabilities is exactly the product rule for the whole collection, which requires mutual independence. Pairwise independence is not enough, as the three-coin example shows.

questions.question: Why do only about 23 people give even odds of a shared birthday among 365 days?
options: Because each new person has a 1/2 chance of matching someone
Because the number of pairs grows like n², so Pr[no match] ≈ e^(−n(n−1)/(2·365)) falls quickly
questions.explanation: There are about n²/2 pairs, each of which could match. Solving e^(−n(n−1)/(2d)) = 1/2 gives n ≈ 1.18√d ≈ 23. Pigeonhole only gives the worst-case guarantee of 366.
